title: Projectile Motion and Its Applications
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version builds projectile motion from the independence of the two components and derives all standard results step by step — the derivation chain NEB expects.

**The governing idea:** horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT. Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity stays constant ($v_x = u\cos\theta$) while the vertical motion is free fall with initial speed $u\sin\theta$. The path is the combination — a parabola.

**Component equations (up positive, launch at angle $\theta$ with speed $u$):** horizontal: $x = (u\cos\theta)t$, $v_x = u\cos\theta$; vertical: $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$.
**Time of flight:** set $y = 0$ on landing: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ — twice the time to the top ($u\sin\theta/g$).
**Maximum height:** at the top $v_y = 0$: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ — vertical throw with initial speed $u\sin\theta$.

**Horizontal range:** $R = v_x T = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$. Since $\sin 2\theta$ peaks at $2\theta = 90°$, **maximum range at $\theta = 45°$**, and complementary angles ($30°$ & $60°$, $15°$ & $75°$) give the SAME range.

**Velocity at any instant:** $v = \sqrt{(u\cos\theta)^2 + (u\sin\theta - gt)^2}$ at angle $\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{u\sin\theta - gt}{u\cos\theta}\right)$ below/above horizontal. On landing, magnitude equals $u$ (symmetry) with direction $-\theta$.
**Trajectory equation:** eliminate $t$: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ — a parabola. Also useful: $R = 4H\cot\theta$ connecting range and height.

**Applications to quote:** cannon/artillery ranges, projectile games (javelin, football), water-fountain arcs, bombing-release problems (bomb keeps the plane's horizontal velocity), and projectile on an inclined plane (extension: $R = \frac{2u^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$ for incline angle $\alpha$ — beyond syllabus but good insight).

**NEB exam focus:** state independence of motions; derive $T$, $H$, $R$; prove max range at 45°; show complementary angles share range; compute velocity (magnitude and direction) at a given time or height; draw the labelled trajectory.
confusion: ❌ 'A projectile's horizontal velocity decreases during flight.' ✅ $v_x = u\cos\theta$ is CONSTANT (no horizontal force in the ideal model); only $v_y$ changes.
❌ 'At the top of the trajectory the velocity is zero.' ✅ Only $v_y = 0$; the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ persists — speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$, the MINIMUM of the flight.
❌ 'The path is part of a circle / straight line decaying.' ✅ The trajectory is a PARABOLA — the graph of $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$.
❌ Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin 2\theta$ in the range. ✅ $R = u^2\sin 2\theta/g$; and $\sin 2\theta$ is maximal at $\theta = 45°$, not $90°$.
❌ 'Complementary angles give different ranges.' ✅ $\sin 2(90°-\theta) = \sin(180°-2\theta) = \sin 2\theta$ — $30°$ and $60°$ land at the SAME spot (the 60° shot flies higher).
❌ Doubling $u$ doubles the range. ✅ $R \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed QUADRUPLES range (and quadruples max height too).
practice: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30°. Find $T$, $H$, $R$ ($g = 10$). — $T = 2$ s; $H = 5$ m; $R = 34.6$ m.
Prove that the speed on landing equals the launch speed, using components at $t = T$.
A projectile has range 100 m and time of flight 4 s. Find its horizontal velocity and launch angle. — $v_x = 25$ m/s; $u_y = gt/2 = 20$ m/s → $\theta = \tan^{-1}(20/25) = 38.7°$.
Two projectiles are fired at 30° and 60° with the same speed 40 m/s. Show both have $R = 141$ m, and compare their maximum heights (1 : 3).

From a 45 m cliff a stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s. When and where does it land? — fall time $t = 3$ s; horizontal landing distance $= 30$ m; impact speed $= \sqrt{10^2 + 30^2} \approx 31.6$ m/s.
universalFacts: Galileo's *Dialogues* (1638) first showed projectile motion is a parabola by superposing uniform horizontal motion with vertical fall — the first known composition of motions.
Artillery fire above ~30 km (Paris Gun, WWI) deviates from the parabola: thin air changes drag and $g$'s direction varies — ideal parabolic flight is a near-Earth, no-air model.
Long-jump athletes take off near 21°, not 45°, because take-off speed itself drops with steeper angles — the real optimum balances range angle against speed loss.
Basketball free throws exploit the high-arc (complementary-angle) region: a steep entry angle enlarges the effective hoop target, even though the flatter shot travels the same distance.
examples: Example 1 (horizontal launch): a stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m tower: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 20/10} = 2$ s; lands 30 m out — vertical fall sets the TIME, horizontal speed sets the DISTANCE.
Example 2 (full trajectory): $u = 25$ m/s at $\theta = 37°$ ($\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$): $T = 3$ s, $H = 11.25$ m, $R = 60$ m — the classic 3-4-5 projectile.
Example 3 (velocity at top): speed at the top $= u\cos\theta = 20$ m/s for the previous shot — the projectile is never at rest.
Example 4 (45° range): maximum range with $u = 30$ m/s is $R_{max} = u^2/g = 90$ m at 45°, with $H = R/4 = 22.5$ m — note $R_{max} = 4H$.
Example 5 (bomb release): a plane at 500 m flying level at 100 m/s releases a bomb — it lands after $t = 10$ s, $500$ m ahead of the release point (it keeps the plane's horizontal velocity).
practiceQuestions: Q1. Show that the path of a projectile is a parabola by eliminating $t$ from the equations of motion.
Q2. Derive $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ and hence prove that the range is maximum for $\theta = 45°$.
Q3. Show that two angles of projection differing by 90° give the same horizontal range.
Q4. A projectile is fired at 50 m/s at 60°. Find (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height, (c) velocity after 2 s.
Q5. Show that the relation between range and maximum height is $R = 4H\cot\theta$, and verify it for $\theta = 45°$ where $R = 4H$.
keyPoints: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent; they share only TIME.
$v_x$ is constant; $v_y$ changes by $g$ every second; the path is a parabola.
At the top: $v_y = 0$, speed $= u\cos\theta$ (minimum), $a = g$ downward.
Landing speed equals launch speed; landing angle equals −launch angle (symmetry).
$R$ is maximum at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges but different heights.
$R \propto u^2$ and $H \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed quadruples both.
summary: Projectile motion is the superposition of constant horizontal velocity and vertical free fall, giving a parabolic path. The three headline results — $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$, $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — all follow from the component equations, with maximum range at 45° and equal ranges at complementary angles. Speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$ (never zero), landing speed equals launch speed, and horizontal-launch problems are handled by letting the vertical fall set the time. These results assume no air resistance and constant $g$.
specialNotes: Note 1: In horizontal-launch problems, get the time from the VERTICAL fall first, then multiply by $v_x$.
Note 2: Memorise $\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$ and $\sin 2\theta$ values for 30°/45°/60° — NEB numericals use them constantly.
Note 3: 'Same range' pairs: compare heights as $\sin^2\theta : \sin^2(90°-\theta)$ — the steeper shot rises 3× higher for the 30°/60° pair.
Note 4: State the assumptions (no air resistance, constant $g$, flat ground) in theory answers — they define the model.
importantStatements: Statement 1: A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent; gravity acts only on the vertical component.
Statement 2: The horizontal velocity of a projectile remains constant throughout the flight (no air resistance).
Statement 3: The trajectory of an ideal projectile is a parabola.
Statement 4: The horizontal range is maximum at 45° and equal for complementary angles of projection.
importantNotes: Note 1: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal: $v = u\cos\theta$ — not zero.
Note 2: Landing speed equals launch speed and the landing angle mirrors the launch angle (energy/symmetry).
Note 3: $R \propto u^2$: small speed increases at launch produce large range gains.
Note 4: For horizontal projection from a height, time of flight depends ONLY on the height: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — for 30° and 60°, $\sin 2\theta = \sin 60° = 0.866$; write the common range instantly.
Trick 2: At 45°, $R = 4H$ — if a question gives one, the other is a division away.
Trick 3: Horizontal launch from height $h$: time $= \sqrt{2h/g}$, landing speed $= \sqrt{v_x^2 + 2gh}$.
Trick 4: Velocity direction at time $t$: $\tan\phi = \dfrac{u\sin\theta - gt}{u\cos\theta}$ — positive above the horizontal, negative below.
Trick 5: In 'bomb released from plane' questions, the bomb retains the plane's horizontal speed — range = plane speed × fall time.
examNotes: Exam Tip 1: Derivations of $T$, $H$ and $R$ from components are standard 4-mark questions — write the two component tables first.
Exam Tip 2: Draw the trajectory with $v_x$ arrows equal everywhere and $v_y$ arrows shrinking/rising — examiners look for the independence idea.
Exam Tip 3: For 'velocity at height h' questions use $v_y^2 = (u\sin\theta)^2 - 2gh$ — avoids solving a quadratic in $t$.
Exam Tip 4: State the no-air-resistance assumption; if a question mentions drag, the parabola model no longer applies.

importantConcepts: Concept 1: Independence of horizontal (uniform) and vertical (accelerated) motions.
Concept 2: Component kinematics — $v_x$ constant, $v_y$ with $-gt$; time is the shared variable.
Concept 4: Symmetry — equal speeds at equal heights; landing mirrors launching.
Concept 5: Trajectory parabola and the $R$–$H$ relation $R = 4H\cot\theta$.
importantTasks: Task 1: Derive $T$, $H$, $R$ from components in writing, then specialise to $\theta = 45°$.
Task 2: Solve ten numericals: horizontal launches, angled launches, and velocity-at-time/height cases.
Task 3: Verify the complementary-angle range equality numerically for 15°/75° with $u = 40$ m/s.
Task 4: Trace the full trajectory table ($x, y, v_x, v_y$ each 0.5 s) for $u = 20$ m/s at 30° and plot it.
Task 5: Explain in words why a horizontally thrown stone and a dropped stone hit the ground together.
